record.narrative: At the first explore stage I registered a broad but powered set of comparisons for the 16 CRISPR dependency outcomes. I prioritized binary predictors with prevalence large enough to provide at least 20 observations in exposed and comparator cells, especially markers with approximately 20-50% exposed prevalence or balanced prevalence, because these give the best early power to detect differences. I selected several higher-variance dependency outcomes (for example outcome_014, outcome_006, outcome_001, outcome_008, outcome_013, and outcome_011) plus several lower-variance but biologically representative dependency outcomes to identify predictors with possible outcome-specific effects. For each mean_difference claim, exposure=1 denotes the presence of the measured marker and comparator=0 denotes absence. Because more negative dependency scores indicate stronger CRISPR dependency, the scientific hypothesis is that the exposed marker is associated with a more negative outcome, i.e. a raw exposed-minus-comparator mean difference below zero. Therefore I registered direction=-1 and anticipated_direction=-1, so a positive signed evidence estimate would indicate support for the hypothesis. I also registered two interaction claims to test whether a binary marker's association is stronger in a predefined high stratum: an interaction for outcome_014 using feature_034 with feature_061 threshold at 50, and an interaction for outcome_006 using feature_045 within feature_002=1 versus its complement. These are exploratory associations in the supplied dataset only, not causal claims. For later appraisal, I will consider an effect scientifically meaningful only if it is in the hypothesized direction, has a 95% interval that is sufficiently away from zero, and has an absolute mean difference large enough to plausibly exceed the 10% relative clinical-significance threshold; given typical outcome magnitudes around 0.25 absolute, I will regard differences of roughly 0.03-0.05 dependency units and especially larger as candidates for acceptance, with uncertainty guiding the final conclusion.

No new evidence is yet available, so I request the full registered initial set of 12 comparisons. This maximizes broad discovery information from the first analysis round: ten main mean_difference tests across diverse outcomes and high-power binary markers, plus two interaction/effect-modification tests. The selected claims all have sufficient cell counts based on their registered exposure definitions, and running all 12 within the limit provides the needed discovery evidence for subsequent appraisal and focused follow-up.

All 12 discovery comparisons were validly analyzed with adequate cell counts. Because every claim used direction -1, positive signed estimates support the hypothesis that exposure=1 is associated with a lower, i.e. stronger, CRISPR dependency score, whereas negative signed estimates oppose the hypothesis. I used an approximate 10% clinical relevance threshold based on 0.1×|outcome/comparator mean|: outcome_014 about 0.009, outcome_006 about 0.018, outcome_001 about 0.042, outcome_008 about 0.028, outcome_013 about 0.027, outcome_011 about 0.030, outcome_016/outcome_007/outcome_012/outcome_002 about 0.025-0.026. None of the discovery 95% Welch intervals excludes zero, so none provides statistically supported evidence for the registered negative association, and with 12 comparisons the risk of overinterpreting marginal point estimates is substantial. For H4, H6, H7, H8, and H10, the upper bound of the hypothesis-direction interval is below the approximate 10% clinical threshold and the point estimates are not supportive; these are reject/closed as not supported in this dataset. H1, H3, H5, H9, H11, and H12 have intervals wide enough to include clinically plausible effects, but the point estimates are small or in the opposite direction and these do not merit immediate follow-up or validation; I closed them as non-conclusive but not priority lines. H2 is the only unresolved active line: feature_060 with outcome_006 has a signed estimate of about +0.019, just above the approximate clinical threshold, but the interval (-0.015 to +0.054) crosses zero. It remains unresolved and active because it is the only broad-screen result with both reasonable precision and a clinically plausible point estimate; future work should refine this marker/outcome pair and consider related outcomes or subgroups rather than immediately accepting the main effect. I did not request validation because no discovery interval excludes null or clinically important effects, and validation based solely on a marginal point estimate would be vulnerable to multiplicity and false-positive inflation. Scientifically, these are associations in the supplied dataset only, not causal claims, and predictor correlations may confound marker effects.

There is no new validation response or due assessment deadline, so the synthesis conclusion is based on the first discovery set. The overall state is negative so far: no claim meets the evidentiary bar for a scientifically meaningful association in this supplied dataset. Several claims are rejected because the hypothesis-direction 95% intervals are compatible with negligible or clinically non-significant effects, while others remain unresolved only because uncertainty is too wide or the point estimate is not compelling. H2, feature_060 compared with its comparator for outcome_006, is the only active unresolved candidate. Its signed estimate of about +0.019 is just around the approximate 10% clinical threshold for outcome_006 (absolute mean around 0.175, so about 0.0175), but its interval crosses zero and the outcome has high residual variance. Because this was discovered among several comparisons and its interval is not decisive, it cannot be accepted or validated on this evidence alone. The next analysis should test whether H2 is a stable marker effect or a chance screen hit by checking whether feature_060 associates coherently with related CRISPR dependency outcomes with better precision, especially outcome_005, outcome_002, outcome_015, and outcome_007. These outcomes have lower variance and approximate 10% thresholds around 0.024-0.025, so they can distinguish a clinically relevant effect from noise if the effect is real and broad. In parallel, I registered interaction tests to see whether the feature_060 effect in outcome_006 is concentrated in feature_002=1 or feature_034=1 strata. These are high-prevalence binary strata and are therefore reasonably powered relative to rarer subgroup splits. I also registered focused outcome_006 tests for other high-power binary predictors, including feature_034, feature_002, feature_045, feature_042, and feature_021. The feature_045 main-effect test is motivated by the earlier H12 interaction, although H12 itself is unresolved with a negative point estimate, so no direction is anticipated. Overall, the plan is targeted follow-up of the sole promising screen result plus a bounded set of related tests, rather than indiscriminate additional testing. Any future acceptance should require either a 95% interval that excludes both zero and the approximate 10% relevance threshold, or at least a sufficiently large point estimate with a lower bound not compatible with negligible clinical effect. These conclusions remain dataset-specific associations and not causal or generalizable claims.

No assessments are due and no new validation has arrived, so this stage registers follow-up and broadening comparisons. The only unresolved active discovery line remains H2: feature_060=1 versus feature_060=0 for outcome_006, signed estimate about +0.019 with a 95% interval crossing zero. Rather than treating that marginal estimate as accepted, I am testing whether it is part of a coherent feature_060 effect across lower-variance dependency outcomes, specifically outcome_003 and outcome_004 in addition to the already registered outcome_005, outcome_002, outcome_015, and outcome_007 comparisons. These lower-variance outcomes have approximate 10% clinical thresholds around 0.017-0.026 and standard deviations near 0.175-0.181, so they can more sharply distinguish a clinically meaningful association from noise. I also registered a systematic high-power screen for two common binary markers, feature_034 and feature_002, across four lower-variance outcomes: outcome_005, outcome_015, outcome_002, and outcome_007. This is scientifically useful because these predictors are prevalent enough to give strong power, and if either marker has a broad dependency-association pattern, it should appear more consistently than a single marginal outcome_006 hit. For these two marker panels I set direction=-1 because that represents the hypothesis that marker presence is associated with stronger CRISPR dependency, i.e. a more negative score, but anticipated_direction=0 because no marker-level effect has yet been established. I added a nominal two-level predictor contrast, feature_054 level_002 versus level_001, on outcome_006; both groups are large enough for a valid Welch comparison, and this broadens beyond numeric binary features. I also added feature_021 on outcome_015 to test an unexamined moderately prevalent binary marker on a lower-variance outcome. All proposed effects are associations in the supplied dataset only. Future acceptance will require a hypothesis-direction interval that is sufficiently away from zero and compatible with at least a 10% relative effect for the relevant outcome, not merely a nominally positive point estimate.

No validation is due and I will not request validation from current evidence. I selected 12 previously registered but untested main-effect claims, prioritizing high-power binary predictors and lower-variance dependency outcomes that can distinguish clinically relevant effects from noise. First, I request all registered lower-variance outcome tests for feature_060: outcome_003, outcome_004, outcome_005, outcome_002, outcome_015, and outcome_007. This is the most focused follow-up of H2: if feature_060=1 is truly associated with stronger dependency, it should appear coherently across related outcomes with similar scale and lower residual variance than outcome_006. Second, I request a high-power marker panel for the two balanced binary predictors feature_034 and feature_002 across three lower-variance outcomes: outcome_005, outcome_015, and outcome_002. These predictors have nearly balanced exposure counts, so each comparison has roughly comparable precision and can provide useful discovery evidence about whether common binary markers have broadly biologically relevant associations rather than isolated high-variance outcome_006 fluctuations. I deferred interactions such as H13/H14 and many outcome_006 marker tests for now because interaction intervals are wider and main-effect coherence across lower-variance outcomes is more informative at this stage. All selected cells are expected to satisfy the minimum cell-count requirement. I will interpret positive signed estimates, because direction=-1, as evidence that exposure is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency, but acceptance will require both statistical precision and clinically meaningful magnitude relative to the approximately 10% outcome-specific threshold. These remain dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable conclusions.

The newly delivered evidence sharply deprioritizes the feature_060 line. All claims used direction -1, so positive signed estimates indicate that exposure=1 is associated with a more negative, i.e. stronger, CRISPR dependency score. For H32/H33/H15/H16/H17/H18, feature_060 tested on lower-variance outcomes produced small positive, small negative, or near-zero estimates, and in every case the 95% interval either crossed zero or its upper bound remained below the approximate 10% clinical relevance threshold. I therefore reject these clinically and statistically unsupported feature_060 effects and close them. This also undermines the prior marginal H2 signal in outcome_006: a real broad marker effect should generally be detectable in several related lower-variance outcomes with good precision, but these follow-up outcomes did not reproduce a coherent feature_060 association. I keep H2 unresolved because its own interval still includes clinically plausible values, but close it as a non-priority line rather than spend validation on it. The most useful new result is H26: feature_034=1 versus 0 on outcome_015 has signed estimate +0.0170 and a 95% interval +0.0017 to +0.0323. It is the only new claim whose interval excludes zero in the hypothesized direction, suggesting a dataset-specific association with stronger dependency. However, I do not accept it as clinically meaningful from discovery evidence alone: the point estimate is only about 6.8% of the outcome mean, below the 10% clinical threshold, and the lower confidence bound is very close to zero. The discovery interval remains compatible with a nonclinical effect. H24 on outcome_005 is similar but weaker: point +0.0102 with lower bound below zero and only a slight upper-bound extension above threshold, so it is unresolved and deferred rather than accepted. Other feature_034 or feature_002 tests on outcome_002 and outcome_015 are null or in the opposite direction and are rejected. I request independent validation for H26 only because it is the sole candidate with a 95% interval excluding zero and a clinically plausible upper bound; independent validation can determine whether this association is robust enough to approach or exceed the clinical threshold. I registered coherence tests for feature_034 across additional low-variance dependency outcomes and one exploratory feature_002 subgroup interaction for the H26 result. Multiplicity is now substantial, correlations among opaque predictors remain unknown, and no claim here should be interpreted as causal or generalizable outside the supplied dataset.

The new validation result changes the conclusion on H26. All claims use direction=-1, so a positive signed estimate means the exposed group has a lower dependency score, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency, than the comparator. H26 tested feature_034=1 versus feature_034=0 on outcome_015. The discovery estimate R21 was modestly positive (+0.0170, about 6.8% relative to the outcome_015 absolute mean) with a 95% Welch interval +0.0017 to +0.0323. That discovery evidence was statistically positive but not clinically decisive because the point estimate was below the approximate 10% clinical threshold of about 0.0250 and the lower bound was compatible with a negligible effect. The independent validation R25 is much weaker: signed estimate +0.00182, about 0.73% of the outcome_015 absolute mean, with an independent interval alpha about 0.004 from -0.0212 to +0.0249. It crosses zero and its upper bound is just below the clinical relevance threshold. Taken with the marginal discovery estimate, the combined evidence does not support a clinically meaningful association between feature_034=1 and stronger outcome_015 dependency. I therefore reject H26 and close the investigation. This failure also deprioritizes other feature_034 coherence tests, because spending further multiplicity on that predictor is less compelling now; I move those untested feature_034 claims to deferred rather than active. Supported findings: none currently meet the acceptance bar for a scientifically meaningful association in the supplied dataset. Negative findings: feature_060 is unsupported as a broad dependency association, especially after tests across lower-variance outcomes produced small, opposite, or non-clinical estimates. feature_002 is unsupported in the outcomes tested so far, with mostly opposite or clinically negligible intervals. feature_034/outcome_015 is rejected clinically after validation failure, and feature_034/outcome_002 was not supported. Unresolved uncertainty remains for feature_034/outcome_005: R19 was a small positive but not statistically precise signal, with interval -0.0057 to +0.0261; it remains low priority and unresolved rather than accepted. Most informative next analysis: avoid spending more capacity on feature_034 and feature_060; pivot to a bounded high-power screen of other binary or two-level predictors with adequate cell counts, especially feature_045, feature_042, feature_021, feature_012, feature_050, and feature_054 level_002 versus level_001, tested on outcome_003 and outcome_015. The existing H35 feature_021/outcome_015 test is made active so it can be part of this 12-comparison priority set. This panel uses lower-variance outcomes with approximate clinical thresholds near 0.025 and reasonably balanced cell sizes, making it better able to distinguish a meaningful association from noise. All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal effects or externally generalizable claims.

There are no assessments due in this stage. The current accepted set is empty, and the most substantial prior candidate, H26, was rejected after independent validation. Therefore, the next exploration should avoid feature_034, feature_060, and feature_002 unless a new independent signal appears, and should instead test additional predictors with adequate cell counts on outcomes where precision is highest. I register two complementary families of new comparisons. First, I add a bounded screen of six additional prevalent binary markers—feature_065, feature_037, feature_027, feature_052, feature_020, and feature_011—on outcome_003 and outcome_015. These outcomes have absolute means near -0.25, so the approximate 10% clinical relevance threshold is near 0.025, and their standard deviations are about 0.18, giving better power for moderate effects than high-variance outcomes such as outcome_006, outcome_001, outcome_014, or outcome_008. The selected markers have prevalence roughly 16%-21%, so exposed cells should comfortably exceed the 20-observation requirement. Second, I register contrasts for feature_055, a four-level nominal predictor whose most frequent level occurs only 519 times, implying that the other three levels should still be large enough for valid Welch comparisons. I compare each non-top level against level_003 on outcome_003 and outcome_015 to detect level-specific associations with dependency score. Finally, I register four exploratory interactions between prevalent binary markers feature_045 or feature_042 and feature_061 ge 50 on outcome_003 and outcome_015. These interactions test whether the exposed-minus-comparator association is stronger in the feature_061 ge 50 subgroup than in its complement. Interactions are underpowered relative to main effects, so they are lower priority and should only be treated as important if the estimate is both precise enough and clinically large. All proposals use direction -1, representing the hypothesis that the exposed category or level is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency. Because no evidence currently identifies the direction for these predictors, anticipated_direction is set to 0 and initial_status is unresolved. For main-effect proposals, a positive signed estimate will mean exposed minus comparator is negative after direction signing. For interaction proposals, a positive signed estimate will mean the exposed-minus-comparator contrast is more negative in the feature_061 ge 50 subgroup than in the complement. Future acceptance will require a hypothesis-direction interval excluding zero and a magnitude compatible with at least a 10% relative difference, roughly 0.025 for these lower-variance outcomes. These remain associations in the supplied dataset only, not causal or generalizable claims.

No assessments are currently due, and there is no new validation to reassess. The current accepted set is empty, and prior validation has effectively closed the strongest earlier candidate involving feature_034, while feature_060 and feature_002 are also deprioritized. I therefore request twelve main-effect discovery analyses that test untested predictors with favorable precision. The highest-priority untested predictor is feature_055: it has four nominal levels, the largest level count is only 519, and the remaining levels must still be large because all level counts are bounded by the maximum and sum to 2000. This makes feature_055 comparisons unusually balanced and gives narrow Welch intervals relative to 20% prevalence binary markers. I request all three non-top feature_055 contrasts versus level_003 on both outcome_003 and outcome_015. These outcomes have similar scale and relatively low variance, with approximate 10% clinical thresholds near 0.025. I also request high-prevalence untested two-level predictors feature_042 and feature_054 on both outcomes. Feature_054 level_002 versus level_001 has an exposed cell of about 578, and feature_042 has about 463 exposed observations, both providing reasonably precise main-effect tests. I include one existing active feature_021 test, H35, to begin evaluating that predictor, and one feature_050 test, H52, because prior discovery evidence for feature_050 was not opposite and its interval upper bound reached clinically relevant territory, although it was not decisive. I deliberately do not request feature_045 at this point because H10 already gave a precise null for outcome_002, reducing its priority relative to untested predictors. Interactions and several new binary expansions are deferred because main effects are more informative at this stage and several expansions have prior evidence in the opposite direction or weaker precision. All selected claims use direction -1, so a positive signed estimate means the exposed group has a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency. For acceptance, I will require the hypothesis-direction interval to exclude zero and an effect magnitude compatible with at least approximately a 10% relative difference, roughly 0.025 for these outcomes. These are dataset-specific associations, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

All claims use direction -1, so a positive signed estimate means the exposed category is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency. For outcome_003 and outcome_015 the absolute outcome means are about 0.25, so the 10% clinical difference threshold is approximately 0.025. No new claim meets the acceptance bar. The feature_055 contrasts are not supportive overall: level_001 vs level_003 is small and imprecise on outcome_003, and the corresponding outcome_015 contrast is in the opposite direction and only borderline for even a modest positive association. level_002 and level_004 vs level_003 are small and mostly opposite on outcome_015 or null on outcome_003. I close the feature_055 line as not clinically supported; H66 remains unresolved rather than rejected because its upper bound crosses the clinical threshold, but it is not worth further investment. The feature_042 and feature_054 main-effect tests are null or opposite and below the clinical threshold, so I reject and close them. The feature_021/outcome_015 test is negative, i.e. opposite to the hypothesis, with a near-null upper bound, and is rejected. The only remaining candidate is H52, feature_050=1 vs 0 on outcome_015: the signed estimate is positive, +0.0176, but that is only about 7% of the outcome_015 absolute mean and the 95% interval still crosses zero, lower bound -0.0015 and upper bound 0.0367. This is compatible with a clinically meaningful effect but does not establish one, and it also has to be interpreted in the context of substantial multiplicity and prior weak positive feature_050 evidence on outcome_012. I do not request independent validation for H52 now because the discovery evidence is borderline and below the clinical point threshold; the prior H26 validation failure also suggests that validation should be reserved for candidates with stronger discovery support or after coherence across related outcomes. Instead, I registered targeted feature_050 coherence tests on other lower-variance dependency outcomes. If these are null, the feature_050 line should be closed; if they show consistent positive estimates, the case for validation becomes stronger. All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable claims, and the comparisons are unadjusted for other measured predictors, so confounding and correlated predictor structure remain possible.

The newly delivered independent validation concerns H7, feature_037=1 versus 0 on outcome_016. All claims use direction -1, so a positive signed estimate would mean exposed cases have a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency. The discovery estimate R7 was opposite to the hypothesis, about -0.0092, with interval -0.0289 to +0.0105. The independent validation R38 is essentially null: -0.0007 with an independent interval -0.0297 to +0.0283. Outcome_016 has an absolute mean of about 0.256, so the approximate 10% clinical threshold is about 0.026. H7 has neither statistical evidence nor a clinically meaningful point estimate, and the validation is extremely imprecise but centered near zero. I therefore retain the reject decision and close H7. The failed validation also deprioritizes untested feature_037 outcomes; I defer them rather than spend capacity there unless a new independent signal appears.

No claim currently meets the acceptance bar. The most useful remaining line is feature_050. H52 on outcome_015 is the only positive candidate with a clinically plausible upper bound: estimate +0.0176, interval -0.0015 to +0.0367, though it is only about 7% of the absolute mean and does not exclude zero. The prior feature_050 test on outcome_012 was also weakly positive, R9: +0.0057, interval -0.0139 to +0.0252. Before validating a single borderline outcome, I am prioritizing coherence across several low-variance dependency outcomes. The registered feature_050 coherence tests now cover outcome_003, outcome_004, outcome_005, outcome_007, and I add outcome_002, outcome_009, and outcome_010 as new claims. Together with outcome_015 and outcome_012 evidence, this provides a focused panel on predictors with reasonable cell counts and approximate clinical thresholds near 0.025. If these are mostly null or opposite, the feature_050 line should be closed. If several are positive and at least one becomes precise enough to cross zero near or above the clinical threshold, validation becomes more compelling. I keep a small complementary marker screen for feature_045, feature_012, and feature_065 on low-variance outcomes, while deferring other binary-marker expansions and interactions that currently lack supportive main-effect evidence. These are dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable conclusions.

No assessments are due and there is no new validation. The accepted set remains empty. The most informative active line is feature_050: H52 on outcome_015 has a positive but imprecise candidate estimate (R37), and H9 on outcome_012 has a weak positive estimate (R9). Before validating a single borderline association, I am extending the feature_050 coherence panel to additional outcomes that are still reasonably measurable: outcome_013, outcome_016, outcome_011, and outcome_008. These extend coverage from the lower-variance panel already registered (outcome_002, outcome_003, outcome_004, outcome_005, outcome_007, outcome_009, outcome_010, outcome_012, outcome_015) to outcomes with somewhat larger variance but still potentially interpretable. If feature_050 shows broadly positive, precise, clinically plausible signals across this panel, validation will be justified; if it is null or mixed/opposite, the feature_050 line should be closed. I also register a focused age-modification interaction for feature_050 on outcome_015, using feature_061 ge 50. This is lower priority because interactions are underpowered, but it is scientifically useful because it tests whether any feature_050 dependency association is concentrated in an older subgroup. Finally, I introduce feature_063, an untested three-level nominal predictor with a large top level (level_001, n=1190) and two non-top levels collectively containing 810 observations, likely providing cells large enough for valid Welch tests. I compare level_002 and level_003 against level_001 on outcome_003 and outcome_015. These outcomes have approximate 10% clinical thresholds near 0.025, and feature_063 may offer better power than low-prevalence binary markers. All feature_050 extension claims use anticipated_direction -1 because the existing weak feature_050 evidence points toward exposed values having lower scores, i.e. stronger dependency, but the result is not yet trusted. New feature_063 claims use anticipated_direction 0 because direction is unknown. For acceptance, I will require hypothesis-direction intervals excluding zero and point estimates or intervals compatible with at least 10% relative differences. These remain dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

No assessments are due and no new validation is currently available. The only active candidate line is feature_050: H52 on outcome_015 gives a positive but imprecise signed estimate (R37), and H9 on outcome_012 gives a weak positive estimate (R9). To avoid validating a single borderline outcome, I request the full remaining feature_050 main-effect coherence panel over all other registered outcomes (H76-H86). These are Welch tests of feature_050=1 versus 0 for each dependency score, all with direction -1, so positive estimates mean exposed observations have more negative scores, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency. This tests whether feature_050 shows a coherent pattern across outcomes with clinically relevant thresholds of roughly 10% of the absolute mean: near 0.025 for outcome_002, outcome_003, outcome_004, outcome_005, outcome_007, outcome_009, outcome_010, outcome_012, and outcome_015, and slightly higher for outcome_008, outcome_011, outcome_013, and outcome_016. I also include H87, a feature_050 by feature_061 ge 50 interaction on outcome_015, because if the main effect is not globally strong, it could still be concentrated in the older subgroup; however, interactions are lower priority and underpowered, so this is an exploratory modifier test rather than a primary acceptability criterion. I do not rerun H9 or H52 because they already have cached discovery evidence. I defer feature_063 and other alternative marker screens this iteration because the highest expected information comes from resolving feature_050 coherence. If the feature_050 panel is mostly null or opposite, close that line and move to feature_063 or remaining binary markers. If several feature_050 outcomes are positive and at least one is precise enough near or above the clinical threshold, request validation on the strongest outcome in the next appraise/synthesis cycle. These are dataset-specific association tests only; acceptance will require hypothesis-direction intervals excluding zero and magnitudes compatible with at least 10% relative differences.

All feature_050 claims use direction -1, so a positive signed estimate means feature_050=1 is associated with a more negative CRISPR dependency score, i.e. stronger dependency. For these dependency outcomes, the absolute outcome means are mostly about 0.25-0.30, so the 10% clinical threshold is approximately 0.025-0.030. No due claim meets the acceptance bar of a hypothesis-direction 95% interval excluding zero with a clinically meaningful magnitude. The opposite-direction results are clinically unsupportive for the claimed positive association: H76 outcome_003 R39 estimate -0.0053, upper 0.0144; H77 outcome_004 R40 estimate -0.0050, upper 0.0141; H78 outcome_005 R41 estimate -0.0055, upper 0.0138; H81 outcome_009 R44 estimate -0.0118, upper 0.0084; H84 outcome_016 R47 estimate -0.0066, upper 0.0130; and H86 outcome_008 R49 estimate -0.0053, upper 0.0218. I reject and close these. The positive but imprecise results are not acceptable: H79 outcome_007 R42 estimate +0.0118; H80 outcome_002 R43 estimate +0.0151; H82 outcome_010 R45 estimate +0.0184; H83 outcome_013 R46 estimate +0.0050; H85 outcome_011 R48 estimate +0.0033. Even the largest point estimate, outcome_010, is only about 7.3% of the absolute mean and its interval crosses zero. Some upper bounds cross the clinical threshold, but given the wide multiplicity, correlated outcomes, unadjusted contrasts, and mixed positive/negative pattern, they do not justify acceptance or validation. I record them as unresolved but closed. H87 is the age subgroup interaction on outcome_015; it is opposite to the positive hypothesis, estimate -0.0273, with wide interval -0.0717 to +0.0171. The result is underpowered and not coherent enough to justify a reverse-claim refinement. I therefore close the feature_050 line overall, including the earlier H9 and H52 as unresolved but closed. I also assess H47 not in this stage because it is a duplicate canonical claim of H76; the due duplicate was assessed as H76. No independent validation is requested because no candidate has discovery evidence strong enough to merit a wider validation interval, especially after the H26/H7 validation failures and the failure of feature_050 coherence across the panel. These remain dataset-specific association tests, not causal or generalizable findings, and they are unadjusted for other measured predictors, which may correlate with feature_050 and contribute to the observed mixed pattern.

H26 is a response deadline involving feature_034=1 versus 0 on outcome_015 with hypothesis direction -1, so a positive signed estimate means feature_034=1 is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency. The original discovery estimate R21 was +0.0170, interval +0.0017 to +0.0323. That excludes zero at 95%, but outcome_015 has absolute mean about 0.2495, so the 10% clinical difference threshold is approximately 0.02495. The discovery point estimate is therefore only about 6.8% relative and does not by itself establish a clinically meaningful difference. The independent validation R25 is essentially null: +0.0018, interval -0.0212 to +0.0249. It neither confirms statistical significance nor a clinically meaningful effect. I therefore retain the reject decision and close H26. This is an important calibration result: a discovery interval can exclude zero while the point estimate remains below the clinical threshold, and independent validation can show that such a borderline discovery is not a reliable association. It argues against accepting discovery-only borderline significance in the remaining search. No claim currently meets the acceptance bar. The feature_050 coherence panel is closed because signs were mixed and no outcome had a clinically meaningful positive signal with interval excluding zero. I am pivoting to nominal variables with reasonably large levels. Existing feature_063 contrasts H88-H91 are already active. To use the next analysis capacity efficiently, I propose feature_048 contrasts, comparing non-top levels level_001 and level_002 against the dominant level_003 on outcome_003 and outcome_015, the two lower-variance dependency outcomes where a clinically meaningful contrast is around 0.025. If feature_063, feature_048, or the remaining active binary-marker tests produce a clean positive signal with lower bound above zero and a magnitude near or above the 10% threshold, that candidate should be considered for independent validation. Otherwise the corresponding predictor lines should be closed. All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal effects or generalizable findings, and the tested contrasts are unadjusted for other predictors or outcome correlations.

No assessments are currently due and no new validation has arrived. I am extending the nominal-variable screen with a feature_063 coherence panel because feature_063 has a large reference level and non-reference levels likely large enough for reliable Welch comparisons, whereas many remaining binary markers are lower prevalence and related low-prevalence markers have generally been null or imprecise. These new claims test all 2000 samples, with feature_063 level_002 or level_003 versus level_001 on outcome_012 and outcome_007. The hypothesis direction is -1, so a positive signed estimate means the exposed level is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency, than level_001. The anticipated direction is 0 because the labels are nominal and no prior evidence favors either exposed level. Falsifiable alternatives are no difference, an opposite direction, a statistically borderline but clinically small difference, or heterogeneity across outcomes or feature_063 levels. outcome_012 and outcome_007 have absolute means of about 0.248 and 0.245, so the 10% clinical threshold is roughly 0.025. Combined with the already active feature_063 claims on outcome_003 and outcome_015, this creates a four-outcome coherence panel for feature_063. To prioritize analysis capacity, I defer the untested binary-marker claims H43, H46, H49, and H54 pending the nominal panels; if feature_063 and feature_048 show clean, clinically meaningful positive signals with lower bounds excluding zero, independent validation will be warranted. If they are null, opposite, or only wide-upper-bound suggestive, those predictor lines should be closed before returning to lower-prior marker screens. These are dataset-specific association claims, not causal or generalizable conclusions.

No assessments are due and no validation response is pending. I am requesting the full currently active nominal-variable panel.
